title: AI and a human each submit a Millennium Prize Problem solution: one relies on Claude to complete a 79-page proof, while the other pulls out a 940-page handwritten draft 12 years in the making

content_html:
Two “answer sheets” in the world of mathematics were placed on the table on the same day. Levent Alpöge, a 34-year-old mathematician, joined forces with a professor at New York University to release a 79-page paper claiming to prove a long-standing Millennium Prize Problem: that the three-dimensional Navier–Stokes equations in the absence of external forces exhibit finite-time blow-up. This problem has stumped the mathematical world for more than a century. It asks whether the equations describing the laws of fluid motion can suddenly “lose control” at some point, with the solution shooting off to infinity. More strikingly, the work was carried out in collaboration with Claude throughout, and the team also released Lean formalization code, letting computers check every line of reasoning for rigor on behalf of humans.

For now, this proof remains in a “pending verification” state. Terence Tao gave a broadly positive assessment: the overall strategy of the proof is clear, but it still needs to be organized into a proper mathematical text. A more critical gap is that the key numerical certificates supporting the proof have not yet been made public—without this data, independent verification cannot even begin, and whether the proof is true or false will have to wait.

On the same day, another mathematician, Alessandro Maria Masullo, produced a work taking a completely opposite route: a 940-page draft proof of the generalized Riemann hypothesis that took nearly 12 years, with no AI used from beginning to end. He framed the public release of this manuscript as a message to colleagues discouraged by AI’s disruption of the rhythm of research—that human researchers are still sticking to their own way of exploring, gnawing through hard problems one step at a time.

But enthusiasm cannot replace rigor. This 940-page manuscript has also been found to contain unresolved issues, and it too must await the verdict of verification. On one side is an AI-assisted, 79-page agile sprint; on the other, a twelve-year solitary, 940-page long march. Both answer sheets appeared on the same day and both have yet to pass final review—the door to the Millennium Prize Problem has not opened yet, but the key to opening it may be being forged at the same time along two completely different paths.
